queries.need: Given a base64 string, check that its length is a multiple of 4 and throw if it isn't. Return [validLen, placeHoldersLen], where validLen is the index of the first '=' (or the full length if there is none), and placeHoldersLen is 0 when there is no '=' and otherwise 4 - (validLen % 4).
queries.description:
This is a helper for decoding base64. It takes a base64-encoded string and works out how much of it is real data and how much is trailing padding.

**Input check:** It first checks that the string's length is a multiple of four. If not, it throws an error saying the string is invalid because its length must be a multiple of 4. No other validation happens. It does not check whether the characters belong to the base64 alphabet.

**Finding the data length:** It looks for the first equals sign, which base64 uses for padding.
- If there is one, everything before it counts as meaningful data.
- If there is none, the whole string counts as data.

Anything after the first equals sign is ignored, even if it isn't padding. This is a deliberate choice so that junk after the padding doesn't affect decoding.

**Computing the padding count:**
- With no equals sign, the padding count is zero.
- Otherwise, it is four minus the remainder of the data length divided by four. This gives the number of characters needed to fill out the last four-character group.

**Return value:** A two-element array holding the data length first and the padding count second.

**Edge cases:**
- An empty string passes the length check and returns zero for both values.
- If the first equals sign lands on a four-character boundary (for example, the string starts with one), the padding count comes out as four, which isn't really valid padding. The function doesn't flag this.
- Passing null or undefined causes a type error when it tries to read the length. It does not produce the custom error message.

queries.need: Read four bytes from a byte array as one big-endian signed 32-bit word, starting at a given offset and wrapping around to the start of the array when needed. Return the word and the offset to use for the next read, like the key/salt word reader in Blowfish/bcrypt key setup.
queries.description:
This routine reads a 32-bit value out of a byte sequence, treating the sequence as circular. It looks like the helper used in Blowfish/bcrypt key setup to pull successive words from a repeating key or salt.

**Inputs:** an array-like collection of byte values and a starting position within it.

**What it does:** It reads four consecutive elements, beginning at the given position. Each element is reduced to its lowest 8 bits. The four bytes are combined in big-endian order: the first byte read becomes the most significant. After each read the position advances by one. When it passes the end of the collection, it wraps back to the beginning.

**Output:** an object with two fields:
- the assembled 32-bit word
- the position just after the last byte consumed, ready for the next call

**Edge cases and quirks:**
- **Signed result.** The value comes from JavaScript bitwise operations, so it is a signed 32-bit integer. If the first byte's high bit is set, the result is negative.
- **Out-of-range elements.** Values outside 0–255, including negative ones, are silently truncated to their low byte instead of being rejected.
- **Short collections.** If there are fewer than four elements, bytes repeat cyclically within one word.
- **Empty collection.** The wraparound divides by zero, so the returned position becomes NaN. Every read yields nothing, which masks to zero, so the word is 0.
- **Bad starting position.** A negative, fractional, or too-large position reads a missing element, which contributes 0. Wrapping only partly corrects this, because the remainder keeps the sign and fraction of the original value.
- **No validation.** Nothing is checked. The only way it throws is if the collection itself is null or undefined.

queries.need: Normalize an array of CSV column definitions into column objects. Null, undefined or false become {disabled: true}, strings and numbers become {name: String(value)}, and plain objects with a string name are passed through as-is. Anything else throws a CSV error: missing column name for objects without a string name, invalid column definition for all other values.

inputs.name: columns
inputs.type: Array<string | number | object | null | undefined | boolean>

queries.description:
This function normalizes a list of column definitions, as used when parsing or generating CSV data. It takes an array-like list and returns a new array of the same length. Each entry in the result is an object describing one column, at the same position as its input.

Each input entry is handled according to its kind:

- **Empty or switched-off entries:** an entry that is undefined, null, or exactly the boolean false becomes an object marking that column as disabled. A disabled column is skipped or ignored.
- **Strings and numbers:** these become an object whose name property holds the value converted to a string. A number like 3 becomes the name "3".
- **Plain objects:** these are checked for a name property that is a string. If it is, the original object is placed into the result as-is, not copied, so any other properties on it are preserved. If the name is missing or not a string, a CSV-specific error is thrown. The error code indicates a missing column name, and the message says a name is required at that position when the column is given as an object.
- **Anything else:** values such as true, functions, or arrays (assuming the object check excludes arrays) cause a different CSV-specific error. Its code indicates an invalid column definition. The message says a string or object literal was expected and includes the offending value serialized as JSON, along with its position.

Other behavior to note:

- Processing stops at the first invalid entry. Entries before it are discarded along with the partial result, since the error propagates.
- The input array itself is never modified.
- Holes in a sparse input array read as undefined, so they become disabled columns.
- An empty input produces an empty array.

queries.need: Format a number as a string left-padded with zeros to a minimum width. A minus sign goes in front of the padded digits and does not count toward the width, and long values are never truncated.
queries.description:
This function formats a number as a string with leading zeros so it reaches a minimum width. It is like zero-padding a day or month to two digits.

**Inputs and output**
- It takes a numeric value and a desired minimum length.
- It returns a string.

**How it works**
1. It records whether the value is negative.
2. It converts the absolute value to its default string form.
3. It adds zeros on the left until that string reaches the requested length.
4. If the original value was negative, it puts a minus sign in front of the padded digits.

For example, negative seven with a length of three becomes "-007".

**Edge cases**
- **Sign isn't counted in the width.** A negative result can be one character longer than requested.
- **Already long enough.** If the digits meet or exceed the requested length, nothing is added and nothing is cut off.
- **Zero or negative length.** These cause no padding.
- **Decimals.** The decimal point and fractional digits count toward the length. For example, 1.5 with a length of five becomes "001.5".
- **Very large or very small values.** These may appear in exponential notation, and that text is padded as-is.
- **Negative zero.** This is not treated as negative, so no minus sign appears.
- **Not-a-number.** This becomes the text for not-a-number, padded with leading zeros if the length allows (e.g., "0NaN" for a length of four).
- **Infinite values.** These become the word for infinity, with a minus sign if negative, and are padded the same way if the length allows.
- **Other types.** Numeric strings are coerced to numbers and handled normally.

**Errors**
- There is no validation, so most unusual inputs produce odd text rather than an error.
- A big-integer value will throw a type error when its absolute value is taken.

queries.need: Compute the Levenshtein edit distance between two strings, meaning the minimum number of single-character insertions, deletions and substitutions needed to turn one into the other. The first string is at most 32 characters, characters are compared as UTF-16 code units, and the caller handles empty inputs separately.
queries.description:
This function computes the **edit distance** (Levenshtein distance) between two strings. That is the minimum number of single-character insertions, deletions and substitutions needed to turn one string into the other. It returns that count as a whole number.

**Approach.** It uses a bit-parallel technique (Myers' algorithm). Each position of the first string is one bit in a 32-bit integer. The function walks the second string one character at a time. At each step it updates two bit masks that track whether neighbouring cells in the distance table go up or down. A running score starts at the first string's length and is moved up or down by one according to the top bit of those masks. After the last character, the score is the distance.

**Shared lookup table.** It relies on a table that lives outside the function and is indexed by character code. Before the main loop, it marks in that table, for each character of the first string, the positions where that character appears. Afterwards it resets those entries to zero, so the table is left clean for the next call. Because the table is shared, the function is not safe to run re-entrantly against the same table.

**Edge cases and limits:**
- **First string longer than 32 characters:** the shifts wrap around, and the result is silently wrong. A caller must enforce the limit, typically by passing the shorter string first and using a different routine for longer inputs.
- **Empty first string:** the result is 0, not the second string's length. Callers are expected to handle empty inputs separately.
- **Character units:** characters are compared as UTF-16 code units. Characters outside the Basic Multilingual Plane therefore count as two units. The external table must be large enough for every code unit that appears, which usually means 65,536 entries.
- **Errors:** there is no input validation. Passing non-strings causes a runtime error when it tries to read lengths or character codes. No errors are thrown deliberately.

queries.need: Escape the special characters in a string, such as converting markup characters to HTML entities, and return the input unchanged (the same value) when it contains nothing that needs escaping.
queries.description:
This function takes a single text value and returns a version of it with certain characters escaped. Which characters count as needing escaping, and what each becomes, are defined outside the function: a pattern for detecting them, a second pattern for finding them, and a callback that produces each replacement.

**How it works**

1. **Quick check:** It first tests whether the input contains any character that needs escaping.
   - If nothing matches, it returns the original input unchanged, as the very same value with no copy made. This avoids the cost of a replacement pass for the common case of clean text.
2. **Replacement:** If something does match, it returns a new string in which every match is swapped for whatever the callback returns. Typically this means turning special characters into safe encoded forms, such as markup entities or backslash sequences.

**Edge cases and errors**

- **Empty or clean strings** come back exactly as given.
- **Non-string inputs:** The detection step converts its argument to text before testing, so it never fails on its own.
  - If a non-string's text form has no special characters, the original non-string value is returned as is, not converted to a string.
  - If its text form does contain special characters, the function then tries to call a string replacement method on the original value. Values without that method, such as numbers, plain objects, `null` or `undefined`, will throw a type error at that point.
- **Global-flag hazard:** If the detection pattern is defined with the global flag, it remembers where its last match ended. Repeated calls could then skip matches and wrongly return unescaped text. Whether this matters depends on how that external pattern is defined.
- The function does no other validation and has no error handling of its own.

queries.need: Iterate over an array-like collection in index order, calling a callback with (value, index, collection) for each element and stopping early only when the callback returns strict false. Return the original collection unchanged in identity, or the null/undefined input as-is.
queries.output: array-like | null | undefined (the same collection reference passed in)
queries.description:
This is an iteration helper that visits each element of an array-like collection in order and supports early exit.

**Inputs:** It takes two arguments: a collection to walk through and a callback to run on each element.

**Behavior:** Starting at the first position, it calls the callback once per element with three arguments:
- the current element's value
- its numeric position
- the whole collection

It stops early if the callback returns exactly the boolean false. Other falsy results, such as zero, an empty string, null or undefined, do not stop the loop. Only a strict false does.

**Return value:** It always returns the same collection it was given, not a copy. This allows chaining. Any changes the callback makes to the collection are visible in the returned value.

**Edge cases:**
- **Missing collection:** If the collection is null or undefined, the length is treated as zero. The callback is never called, and the null or undefined value is returned unchanged.
- **Length is read once:** The length is captured before the loop starts. Adding elements during iteration won't extend the loop. Removing elements can cause the callback to receive undefined for positions that no longer exist.
- **Sparse arrays:** Holes are not skipped. The callback is called for them with an undefined value.
- **Array-like objects:** Any object with a numeric length and indexed entries, such as a string or an arguments object, is iterated the same way.

**Errors:** It does no validation or error handling of its own. If the callback is not callable and there is at least one element, a type error is thrown on the first call. Any exception thrown by the callback propagates immediately and ends the iteration.

queries.need: Look up a named property on a metrics object and return it if truthy; otherwise return the same-named property from a tracing object as-is, which may be falsy or undefined. Throw if the metrics object is null or undefined, or if the tracing object is null or undefined and gets consulted.
queries.description:
This is an arrow function that takes no arguments. Each time it is called, it reads a same-named property from two objects defined outside it. The first object appears to handle measurement collection, and the second appears to handle request tracing. The property name matches the name the function itself is assigned to.

**What it returns**
- If the first object's property holds a truthy value, it returns that value right away and never reads the second object.
- Otherwise it returns whatever the second object's property holds, exactly as is. That may be a falsy value or undefined, since nothing checks it.

**Edge cases and errors**
- **Falsy values fall through.** A deliberately set falsy value on the first object is treated as missing, and the second object's value is used instead. This applies to `0`, an empty string, `false`, `null`, or `NaN`.
- **Values are read at call time.** The lookup happens on every call, so later changes to either object show up in the result.
- **Missing first object throws.** If the first outer object is `null` or `undefined` when the function runs, it throws a `TypeError`.
- **Missing second object sometimes throws.** If the second outer object is `null` or `undefined`, it throws only when the first object's value was falsy and the second lookup is reached.
- **Undeclared names throw.** If either outer name was never declared, it throws a `ReferenceError` when evaluation reaches it.
- **No error handling or defaults.** The function does not catch errors or supply a default value.
- **No binding or calling.** It returns the property's value itself. If that value is a function, it is not bound to its owning object and not invoked.

queries.need: Parse a human-readable duration string such as "2 days", "1.5h" or "-3 weeks" into milliseconds. Return undefined for malformed, unrecognized or over-long (more than 100 characters) input, and never throw.
queries.description:
This converts a human-readable duration into a number of milliseconds. Examples are "2 days", "1.5h", "-3 weeks" or "100".

**Input**
- It accepts any value and turns it into a string first.
- If that string is longer than one hundred characters, it returns nothing (undefined). This guards against costly matching on very long input.

**Format it accepts**
The whole string must match this pattern:
- A number, which may be negative and may have a decimal part. Forms like ".5" with no leading digit are allowed.
- Optional spaces.
- An optional unit word, matched without regard to case.

Recognized units come in long, plural and abbreviated forms:
- milliseconds: also "msec", "ms"
- seconds: also "sec", "s"
- minutes: also "min", "m"
- hours: also "hr", "h"
- days: also "d"
- weeks: also "w"
- years: also "yr", "y"

If there is no unit, the number is treated as milliseconds.

**Output**
It multiplies the number by the size of the unit in milliseconds and returns the result. The unit sizes come from constants defined elsewhere. A year is presumably about 365.25 days.

**When it returns nothing**
- The input contains extra text, has a leading plus sign or uses scientific notation.
- There is leading or trailing whitespace.
- The unit is not recognized.

It never throws an error. Bad input simply produces undefined.

queries.need: Check whether a semver comparator object is the special 'matches nothing' comparator, meaning its value field is exactly the string "<0.0.0-0" under strict equality with no normalization.
queries.description:
This is a one-line arrow function. It takes a single object and returns true or false.

It checks whether the object's text field is exactly the string "less than 0.0.0-0". In semantic versioning that string is a deliberately impossible range. Zero point zero point zero with the lowest prerelease tag is the smallest version that can exist, so nothing can be below it. The constraint therefore matches no version at all, and libraries like semver use it as a marker for an empty or unsatisfiable set. So the function answers one question: "is this comparator the one that matches nothing?"

Edge cases and errors:

- **Exact comparison only.** The check uses strict equality, with no trimming or normalization. Any difference in whitespace, letter case, or formatting (for example, a version without the prerelease tag) returns false, even if it means the same thing.
- **No type coercion.** If the field holds a non-string value, the result is false.
- **Missing field.** If the object has no such field, the value is undefined, so the result is false.
- **Bad input.** If the argument is null or undefined, reading the field throws a TypeError. Nothing in the function guards against this or catches it.
- **No side effects.** It doesn't modify its input or anything else.

queries.need: Topologically sort a list of items given directed pairs [before, after], returning every item ordered so each pair's first element comes earlier than its second. Throw if a pair names an item not in the list or if the pairs form a cycle, including a self-loop.
queries.description:
This function performs a **topological sort**. It takes two inputs:

- a list of items
- a list of directed pairs, each saying the first item must come before the second

It returns a new array with every item from the list, ordered so that for every pair, the first element appears earlier than the second.

**How it works**

1. It builds two lookup structures with helper routines. One maps each item to the set of items it points to. The other maps each item to its position in the input list.
2. It checks every pair up front. If either end of a pair is not in the item list, it throws an error saying an unknown node appeared in the edges. No sorting is attempted in that case.
3. It runs a depth-first traversal, starting from items at the end of the list and working backward.
   - For each unvisited item, it marks the item as visited.
   - It then recursively visits every item that the current one points to, taking them in reverse order.
   - Once all of an item's descendants are placed, the item itself goes into the result array, which is filled from the back toward the front.
   - As a result, each item lands ahead of everything that depends on it.
4. While descending, it tracks the chain of items on the current path. If it reaches an item already on that path, there is a loop, and it throws an error saying there is a cyclic dependency. Where possible, the message includes a JSON rendering of the offending item. If that item cannot be serialized (for example, it contains circular references), the message is left without it.
   - A pair connecting an item to itself counts as a cycle.
5. As a secondary safeguard, reaching an item that is not in the item list during traversal throws an error naming the unknown item.

**Edge cases**

- An empty item list produces an empty array.
- Items with no pairs are still included in the output, in positions determined by the traversal order.
- Visited status is tracked by list position. If the same item appears more than once in the input list, the result can be inconsistent. Some positions may be skipped while others hold the duplicate.
- Because the traversal is recursive, a very long chain of dependencies could exceed the call stack limit.

queries.need: Parse a hyphenated 8-4-4-4-12 hex UUID string into its 16 raw bytes in big-endian order, accepting upper- or lowercase hex. Throw a TypeError if the string is not a valid UUID.
queries.description:
This function converts a standard 128-bit unique identifier, written in its usual hyphenated text form (8-4-4-4-12 hexadecimal digits), into its raw binary form: a typed array of 16 unsigned bytes.

**Input:** a single string expected to be a correctly formatted identifier, for example `"f81d4fae-7dec-11d0-a765-00a0c91e6bf6"`.

**Validation and errors:** Before doing anything else, it passes the string to a separate, imported validation routine. If that check fails, it throws a type error whose message says the identifier is invalid. It does no other checking of its own and relies entirely on that validator to guarantee the format.

**Conversion:** It reads the five hexadecimal groups from fixed character positions, skipping the hyphens, and parses each as a number. It then splits each number into bytes, most significant byte first (big-endian):
- The first group (8 digits) becomes 4 bytes.
- The second, third and fourth groups (4 digits each) become 2 bytes each.
- The last group (12 digits) becomes 6 bytes.

The last group is 48 bits, which is wider than JavaScript's 32-bit bitwise operators can handle. So the function uses plain division to extract the top two bytes of that group. It then uses shifts and masks for the lower four bytes, which works because bitwise operations only keep the low 32 bits.

**Output:** a new 16-byte array of bytes in the same order as the hex digits appear in the text. Hex parsing accepts both uppercase and lowercase letters.

queries.need: Return the type name of any value as a string, like the built-in typeof operator, but also report "symbol" for polyfilled symbol instances when native symbols are missing.
queries.description:
This is a compatibility helper, of the kind a transpiler injects, that returns the type name of any value as a string. It works like the language's built-in type-checking operator, but also gives the right answer for symbols in environments where symbols are only polyfilled.

**Input and output:** It takes one value of any kind and returns a string such as "string", "number", "object", "function", "undefined", "boolean", "bigint" or "symbol".

**How it works:** The first time it runs, it checks whether the environment supports symbols natively. That means the global symbol constructor exists as a function and its built-in iterator key is reported as a real symbol.

- **Native support:** It switches to a simple version that just returns the built-in operator's result.
- **No native support (or a polyfill):** It switches to a version that first checks whether the value is a polyfilled symbol. A value counts as one if it is truthy, a global symbol constructor exists, the value was built by that constructor, and the value is not the constructor's prototype object. If so, it returns "symbol". Otherwise it falls back to the built-in operator.

After choosing, it replaces itself with the chosen version, so later calls skip the environment check entirely. It then calls that version on the original value and returns the result.

**Edge cases:**
- Falsy values such as null, zero and empty strings skip the symbol check. Null still comes back as "object", matching the built-in operator.
- The prototype object of the symbol constructor is deliberately not reported as a symbol.
- It never throws for any input.

queries.need: Render any value as indented (two-space) JSON text, then strip the double quotes from object property names so the output looks like a JavaScript object literal. Throws if the value cannot be serialized to a string (undefined, function, symbol, circular, bigint).
queries.description:
This takes any value and returns a text rendering of it. The result looks like a JavaScript object literal: indented, but with the double quotes stripped from property names.

**How it works**

1. It serializes the input with the standard JSON serializer, indenting with two spaces per nesting level.
2. It scans the result for any run of non-quote characters wrapped in double quotes and immediately followed by a colon. In each match it removes the two quotes and keeps the text and colon.

For an ordinary object, the keys come out bare while string values keep their quotes. A nested object with a key of `name` and a value of `Bob` would appear as `name: "Bob"` on its own indented line.

**Edge cases and errors**

- **Primitives:** Numbers, booleans, null and plain strings pass through as their normal JSON text, since none of them has a key.
- **Inputs that serialize to nothing:** If the input is undefined, a function or a symbol, the serializer produces no string. The text replacement step is then attempted on a missing value, which throws a type error. Nothing is caught, so the error reaches the caller.
- **Serializer errors:** Circular references and big integer values make the serializer throw, and those errors propagate unchanged.
- **Unsafe keys:** Keys are unquoted even when they are not valid identifiers, such as keys with spaces, hyphens, or a leading digit. The output may therefore not parse as JavaScript.
- **Keys left quoted:** An empty-string key keeps its quotes, because the pattern needs at least one character. Keys containing escaped quotes are not matched cleanly and may be mangled.
- **Corrupted string values:** The pattern does not know what is a key and what is inside a string. If a string value contains a quoted word followed by a colon (escaped as `\"` in the JSON), part of that value can match and be altered. One example is text that says *he said "hi": then left*.
- **Not valid JSON:** The result is meant for display or code generation, not for parsing back as JSON.

queries.need: Compute the number of bytes a Base64 string decodes to using only its length and trailing '=' padding, without decoding. Throw if the length is not a multiple of four.
queries.description:
This function takes a Base64-encoded string and returns how many bytes it decodes to. It works this out from the string's length alone and never decodes anything.

**How it works**

1. A helper splits the input into two counts:
   - the number of meaningful characters before any trailing `=` padding;
   - the number of padding positions (0, 1, or 2).
2. It adds these two counts back together, which gives the full padded length, and multiplies by three-quarters. Every four Base64 characters encode three bytes.
3. It subtracts the padding count, because each padding character means one fewer real byte in the final group.

For example, an eight-character string with no padding gives 6 bytes. An eight-character string ending in two `=` signs gives 4 bytes.

**Edge cases and errors**

- **Validation:** this function does no checking of its own. All validation happens in the helper. In the widely used library this pattern comes from, the helper throws an error if the input length isn't a multiple of four. If so, malformed lengths cause an exception rather than a wrong answer.
- **Empty string:** the result is 0.
- **Invalid characters:** these are not checked. Only the length and the position of the first `=` are considered, so a string with bad characters but a valid length still gets a byte count.
- **Unusual padding:** if `=` appears early or the padding looks odd, the count is based on wherever the first `=` sits.

queries.need: Encode the first `count` bytes of a byte array as an unpadded bcrypt-style base64 string using the alphabet `./A-Za-z0-9`. Each value is masked to its low 8 bits, and the function throws if `count` is zero or less, or larger than the array length.
queries.description:
This function encodes a run of bytes as a base64-style string. It takes two inputs: an array-like sequence of byte values, and a count of how many of those bytes to encode, starting from the beginning.

**Validation:** Before doing any work, it checks the count. If the count is zero or negative, or larger than the sequence's length, it throws an error whose message names the bad count.

**Encoding:** It walks through the bytes in groups of three. Each value is masked to its low eight bits, so out-of-range numbers are truncated rather than rejected. Every group of three bytes, 24 bits in all, becomes four 6-bit values. Each 6-bit value is turned into a character by looking it up in a 64-character alphabet table defined outside the function.

**Leftover bytes:** If the count is not a multiple of three, the final partial group is handled without padding:
- One leftover byte produces two characters.
- Two leftover bytes produce three characters.
- No `=` padding characters are added.

**Result:** It returns all the characters joined into one string.

The output follows whatever alphabet the external table holds. This unpadded style with a custom alphabet is typical of bcrypt's base64 variant, not standard base64.

queries.need: Check whether a value is a non-null, non-array object (typeof 'object'), such as a record or dictionary. Functions, primitives, null and arrays give false; Dates, Maps and class instances give true.
queries.description:
This function takes a single value of any kind and returns a boolean. It answers whether the value is a non-list, non-empty structured value, the sort you would use as a dictionary or record of named properties.

It returns true only when all three of these hold:

1. The language's built-in type check classifies the value as a structured, non-primitive value.
2. The value is not the special "no value" marker. The language's type check also reports that marker as structured, so it has to be excluded explicitly.
3. The value is not a list.

Everything else yields false: numbers, strings, booleans, undefined, symbols, big integers, the empty marker, and any list.

**Edge cases:**
- **Functions** return false, because the type check reports them as their own category.
- **Dates, regular expressions, maps, sets, class instances, boxed primitives and records with no prototype** all return true. The function only checks the broad category, so it doesn't distinguish plain literal records from other structured values.
- **List-like values that aren't real lists**, such as typed numeric buffers or the special argument collection, return true.
- **Values from another execution realm** (such as a separate frame) are handled correctly, because the list check works across realms.

**Errors:** The function never throws and has no side effects.

queries.need: Return a new date shifted forward or backward by a whole number of calendar days in local time, keeping the wall-clock time the same across DST changes and leaving the original date unchanged. A non-numeric day count yields an invalid date rather than throwing.

inputs.name: options
inputs.type: object (optional, may carry a context/constructor for the result date type)

queries.description:
This function shifts a calendar date forward or backward by a whole number of days. It is the compiled form of a date-library helper that adds days.

**Inputs**
- A date, which may be a date object, a timestamp number, or anything the library's date-normalizing helper accepts.
- A day count, which can be negative to move backward.
- An optional settings object. It can carry a context or constructor that controls what kind of date object is produced, which is useful for time-zone-aware date types.

**What it does**
1. It converts the incoming date into a fresh date object, using the context from the settings if one is given. Because this is a copy, the caller's original value is not changed.
2. If the day count is not a number, it returns an invalid date (one holding a "not a number" time value). That result is built with the same constructor as the context or the original input, so the output type matches what the caller expects.
3. If the day count is zero, it returns the copied date unchanged. This is deliberate: on daylight-saving transition days, re-setting the day-of-month can nudge the clock time during the hour before the change, and skipping the operation avoids that.
4. Otherwise, it moves the copy's day-of-month by the given amount in local time and returns the copy. The built-in date rollover handles crossing month and year boundaries. Working in calendar days rather than adding fixed 24-hour blocks keeps the wall-clock time the same across daylight-saving changes.

**Edge cases**
- Fractional amounts are not rounded here. They are passed to the native day-setting method, which truncates them.
- An input date that is already invalid stays invalid.
- The function does not throw errors. Bad input shows up as an invalid date in the result.

queries.need: Compute the Levenshtein edit distance between two strings: the minimum number of single-character insertions, deletions and substitutions that turn the first into the second. It should handle long strings (over 32 characters) and compare by UTF-16 code units.

args: kitten sitting on the mat today!!
sitting kitten on the mat today!

queries.description:
This function computes the **Levenshtein edit distance** between two strings: the minimum number of single-character insertions, deletions and substitutions needed to turn one into the other. It returns that count as a non-negative integer.

**Method.** It uses a bit-parallel algorithm (Myers' method) extended to strings longer than 32 characters. 32 is the width of one machine-word bitmask.

- The first argument is the "pattern." It is split into consecutive 32-character blocks.
- For each block, the function fills a shared, externally defined lookup table. The table is indexed by character code. Each entry gets a bit mask marking where that character appears in the block.
- It then sweeps over every character of the second argument. Vertical difference bits are kept in two 32-bit words. Horizontal differences between blocks are passed along in two arrays of carry bits, one bit per text position, packed 32 to a word.
- After each block, the table entries it touched are reset to zero, so the table is left clean for the next block or the next call.
- The final block also tracks a running score. The score starts at the pattern's length and goes up or down by one at each text position, based on the top bit of the horizontal differences. That final value is returned.

**Assumptions and edge cases:**
- The lookup table is not created here. It must already exist, be large enough for every character code that appears, and be all zeros on entry. If it is missing, the function throws a reference error. If it holds leftover bits, the result will be wrong.
- Characters are compared as UTF-16 code units. A character outside the Basic Multilingual Plane counts as two units, not one.
- The routine is meant for a non-empty pattern, and in practice for patterns longer than 32 characters. An empty pattern is not handled specially and gives a meaningless result.
- An empty second string returns the pattern's length, which is correct.
- There is no input validation and no error reporting. The only possible error is the missing-table failure described above.

queries.need: Normalize a JSON Pointer given as a string or an array into an array of path segments. A string is split on '/' and must start with '/' or be empty; the leading empty segment is kept and no ~0/~1 unescaping is done. An array is returned unchanged if every element is a string or number, and any other input throws.
queries.description:
This function normalizes a JSON Pointer into a list of path segments, accepting either a textual or an already-split form.

**Text input.** It breaks the text apart at every forward slash.

- If the first piece is empty, it returns the full list of pieces. That happens when the text begins with a slash, or when the text is itself empty.
- The leading empty piece is kept, so the slash-prefixed form `/a/b` becomes an empty string followed by the segments `a` and `b`.
- An empty input yields a list holding one empty string.
- It does not decode the standard escape sequences for tilde and slash. Segments come back exactly as written.
- If the text does not start with a slash, it throws an error saying the pointer is invalid.

**Array input.** It checks every element.

- If every element is a string or a number, it returns the same array object it was given. It does not copy it or change it.
- If any element is some other type (an object, a boolean, null, undefined, and so on), it throws an error. The message says the pointer is invalid and that each segment must be a string or a number.
- An empty array passes and is returned as is.

**Any other input** (a number, null, undefined, a plain object, and so on) throws the generic invalid-pointer error.

queries.need: Filter a list-like collection with a predicate called as (element, index, collection), returning a new array of the elements whose result is truthy, in their original order. A null or undefined collection gives an empty array, and holes are visited as undefined.
queries.description:
This function filters a list. It takes a list-like collection and a test function, and returns a new list containing only the elements that pass the test.

**Inputs**
- A list, or anything with a numeric length and indexed elements.
- A test function. It is called once per element with three arguments: the element, its position, and the whole collection.

**Output**
- A brand-new list of every element for which the test returned a truthy value.
- Elements keep their original order and are packed together with no gaps.
- The original collection is never modified.

**Behavior and edge cases**
- **Missing collection:** If the collection is null or undefined, it is treated as empty and an empty list is returned. The test function is never called.
- **Truthiness:** Any truthy return from the test keeps the element, and any falsy return drops it. The result does not need to be strictly true or false.
- **Fixed length:** Elements are visited in ascending position order from the start. The length is read once at the beginning, so if the test adds elements during the run, those extras are ignored. If the test removes elements, later positions may be read as undefined and passed to the test.
- **Sparse lists:** Empty slots are still visited and passed to the test as undefined. This differs from the built-in filtering method, which skips holes.
- **Errors:** The function does no validation and has no error handling of its own. If the test is not callable, it throws as soon as the first element is reached. Any exception thrown by the test propagates immediately and stops the iteration.

queries.need: Check whether a warning identifier has not yet been recorded in an externally defined collection (a Set) of already-issued warnings, so each warning is shown only once. It is read-only and never adds the value. Matching follows Set semantics: primitives by value, objects by identity, NaN equals NaN, and no type coercion. The examples assume the collection already contains "deprecated-api" and the number 1.
queries.description:
This is a one-line predicate. It takes a single value, usually an identifier for a warning or message, and returns a boolean. The answer is true if that value has not yet been recorded in a collection of already-issued warnings defined outside the function. It is false if the value is already recorded. It answers "should this still be shown?" so callers can emit each warning only once.

**Behavior and edge cases**

- **Read-only:** It only checks membership and never adds the value. Calling it repeatedly with the same input keeps returning true until some other code records that value.
- **How matches are judged:** If the outside collection is a standard Set or Map, matching uses the same rules as those structures:
  - Primitives match by value.
  - Objects and arrays match only by identity, not by content.
  - NaN counts as equal to NaN.
  - Positive and negative zero are treated as the same.
  - No type conversion happens, so the number 1 and the string "1" are different entries.
- **Missing or unusual input:** If nothing is passed, the check is made against undefined. It returns false only if undefined itself was recorded.
- **Errors:** The function has no error handling of its own.
  - If the outside collection doesn't exist when the function runs, a reference error is thrown.
  - If the collection exists but has no membership-check method, a type error is thrown.

queries.need: Format a millisecond duration as a compact string using the largest unit (d, h, m, s) whose threshold the absolute value meets, rounded to the nearest whole number. Values under one second are returned unrounded with an 'ms' suffix.
queries.description:
This function takes a duration in milliseconds and returns a compact, human-readable string that expresses it in the largest fitting unit, followed by a one- or two-letter suffix.

**How it works**

1. It takes the absolute value of the input, so negative durations are classified by their magnitude.
2. It checks unit thresholds from largest to smallest: days, then hours, then minutes, then seconds. These thresholds come from constants defined outside the function, presumably the number of milliseconds in each unit.
3. At the first threshold the magnitude meets or exceeds, it divides the original signed value by that unit and rounds to the nearest whole number. It then appends the unit's suffix: "d", "h", "m" or "s".
4. If the magnitude is under one second, it returns the raw value unchanged with "ms" appended. No rounding happens in this case.

**Examples**

- Ninety seconds' worth of milliseconds becomes "2m", because 1.5 rounds up.
- 500 becomes "500ms".
- 1.5 becomes "1.5ms", since fractional values below a second keep their fraction.

**Edge cases and errors**

- **Negative values** keep their sign, for example "-3h".
- **Rounding** uses the language's standard behavior, where exact halves round toward positive infinity. So a negative half-way value rounds toward zero, for example -1.5 hours gives "-1h" rather than "-2h".
- **Rounding can reach the next unit without switching to it.** Just under a full hour can produce "60m" instead of "1h".
- **Days are the largest unit.** Very large durations come out as large day counts, never weeks or years.
- **No validation or exceptions.**
  - Not-a-number input fails every comparison and returns "NaNms".
  - Infinity returns "Infinityd".
  - Non-numeric input is coerced by the arithmetic and comparisons, which can give odd results. For example, a numeric string under a second is returned with "ms" concatenated directly onto the original text.

queries.need: Check whether an object's `value` property is strictly an empty string. No trimming and no type coercion; it throws if the object itself is null or undefined.
queries.description:
This is a one-line predicate. It takes a single object, typically something like a form field or input control, and returns a boolean saying whether that object's stored value is exactly an empty string.

**Return value**

- It returns true only when the value is a string with zero characters.
- The comparison is strict, so no type conversion happens. It returns false for:
  - a missing or undefined value
  - a null value
  - the number zero
  - false
  - an empty array
  - a string that contains only spaces or other whitespace

**Edge cases and errors**

- It does not trim whitespace, so a field containing a single space counts as not empty.
- It does not check its input. If the argument is null or undefined, reading the property throws a type error.
- Any other kind of argument, including a primitive like a number or a string, simply produces false because it has no such property.
- It has no side effects and does not change the object it receives.

queries.need: Given a list of edges (each a pair of endpoints), return a new array of every distinct endpoint, in order of first appearance. Each edge contributes its first endpoint, then its second, and equality follows JavaScript Set semantics.
queries.description:
This function takes a list of edges, where each edge is a pair of endpoints, and returns a new array of every distinct endpoint in the list. In graph terms, it collects all the nodes mentioned by a set of edges.

**How it works**

- It walks through the edges in order. For each one it records the first endpoint, then the second.
- Duplicates are dropped. The result lists each endpoint once, in the order it first appeared.
- Equality follows the rules of JavaScript's built-in set:
  - Primitives are compared by value.
  - Not-a-number counts as equal to itself.
  - Positive and negative zero count as the same value.
  - Objects are compared by identity, so two separate objects with the same contents both appear.
- The input is not modified.

**Edge cases**

- **Empty list:** returns an empty array.
- **Input without a length (such as a plain object or a number):** the loop never runs, so it returns an empty array.
- **Missing input (null or undefined):** throws a type error when reading the length.
- **Missing edge entry (a null or undefined item in the list):** throws a type error when reading its endpoints.
- **Edge with fewer than two entries:** the missing endpoint is read as undefined, and undefined is included in the result.
- **Edge with more than two entries:** anything past the first two is ignored.
- **Edge given as a string:** its first two characters are treated as the endpoints.

There is no validation beyond these behaviors.

queries.need: Convert a version-1 (time-based) UUID into the equivalent version-6 UUID by reordering the timestamp bits so the most significant come first, and set the version to 6. Return the same form as the input: a hyphenated string for a string, or 16 raw bytes for bytes.
queries.description:
This function converts a time-based UUID from the older version-1 layout into the newer version-6 layout. It returns the result in the same form it was given.

**Input**
It accepts one argument, which can be either:
- a UUID written as a text string, or
- a UUID already held as a sequence of raw bytes.

**Behavior**
1. If the input is text, it is first parsed into its 16 raw bytes. If the input is already bytes, it is used as-is.
2. A helper then rearranges those bytes from the version-1 layout into the version-6 layout. Version 6 holds the same timestamp information as version 1, but orders it with the most significant time bits first, so the identifiers sort chronologically. The helper also marks the result as version 6.
3. The output matches the input's form:
   - text in gives text out, formatted in the usual hyphenated style;
   - bytes in gives bytes out.

**Edge cases and errors**
- **Malformed text:** the parsing step will typically throw if the string is not a valid UUID.
- **Byte input is not checked:** no validation is done on byte input here, so malformed or wrongly sized data passes straight to the conversion helper.
- **Version is not verified:** the function does not check that the input really is a version-1 UUID. Feeding it some other version would still produce a rearranged result, but that result would be meaningless.
- **Unchecked formatting:** when turning the result back into text, it uses a formatter that skips validation. It relies on the conversion having produced well-formed bytes.

queries.need: Convert a module value into an ES-module-style namespace object, the way `import * as ns` interop does. If the value is already marked as an ES module and the flag is off, return it unchanged. Otherwise build a prototype-less wrapper with the value under "default" and its own enumerable properties copied over, keeping getters live and caching wrappers per flag.
queries.description:
This is a module-interop helper, the kind a transpiler emits so that "import everything from a module" works when the module may be either a native ES module or an older CommonJS-style export.

**Inputs and output**

It takes two arguments: a module value and an optional flag. It returns a namespace-like object.

**On its first call, it replaces itself**

The first time it runs, it checks whether weak maps are available. If they are, it creates two private caches, one for each setting of the flag. It then overwrites itself with an inner version that captures those caches, and hands the original arguments to that inner version. Every later call goes straight to the inner logic.

**What the inner logic does**

1. **Already an ES module.** If the flag is off and the value is truthy and marked as an ES module, the value is returned unchanged.
2. **Building a wrapper.** Otherwise it prepares a fresh object with no prototype. The original value is placed under the "default" key.
3. **Primitives.** If the value is null, or is neither an object nor a function, the wrapper is returned right away, holding only that default entry.
4. **Caching.** If weak maps exist, it picks the cache that matches the flag.
   - If this value was wrapped before, the stored wrapper is returned. Repeated imports therefore yield the same object.
   - Otherwise the new wrapper is stored before its properties are copied. Storing it first means circular references resolve to the same, partially built wrapper instead of looping forever.
5. **Copying properties.** It walks every enumerable key of the value, skipping "default" and any inherited keys.
   - If a key is defined by a getter or setter, the full descriptor is copied over, so the accessor stays live rather than being read once.
   - Plain data properties are copied by value.
6. **Result.** It returns the filled-in wrapper.

**Edge cases**

- Without weak map support, nothing is cached: each call builds a new wrapper, and circular structures get no special handling.
- Setting the flag forces wrapping even when the value is marked as an ES module, and those wrappers are cached separately from the unflagged ones.
- The function never throws on its own. Any error would come only from getters on the source value, or from the external type-checking helper it calls.

queries.need: A zero-argument getter that returns the currently active global error-message map, i.e. the custom function that turns validation issues into readable messages. It returns the live stored reference: the override if a setter replaced it, otherwise the module's initial default. It does no validation and never throws.
queries.output: function | undefined (whatever value the module-level override variable currently holds)
queries.description:
This function takes no arguments and returns whatever value a module-level variable currently holds. Judging by that variable's name, it is the active override for the error-message mapping, meaning the custom function that turns validation issues into human-readable messages. This pattern matches a schema-validation library's getter for its globally configured message formatter.

It returns a live reference to the stored value, not a copy. If a setter elsewhere in the module has replaced the override, this function returns the new one; otherwise it returns the default the module started with.

On edge cases and errors:

- **No validation or fallback:** It does nothing beyond the lookup. If the stored value was never initialized or was set to something empty, that is exactly what callers receive.
- **No errors thrown:** Since it only reads a variable already in scope, it cannot fail.

queries.need: Compute the decoded byte length of a base64 string from its count of meaningful characters and its count of padding characters, as (valid + padding) * 3 / 4 - padding. The string argument is ignored, and nothing is validated or rounded.
queries.description:
This is a helper for base64 decoding. It calculates how many raw bytes an encoded string will produce.

**Inputs:** It takes three arguments:
- the encoded string itself, which is ignored
- the count of meaningful characters before any trailing padding
- the count of padding characters

**Calculation:** It adds the two counts to get the full padded length, multiplies by three, and divides by four, since every four encoded characters represent three bytes. It then subtracts the padding count, because each padding character means one fewer real byte in the final group.

**Output:** A number giving the decoded byte length. For example, with two padding characters and a total of eight characters, the result is six minus two, which is four bytes.

**Edge cases and errors:**
- It does no validation, rounding, or type checking.
- It assumes the caller has already split the length correctly into meaningful characters and padding (zero, one, or two).
- If the combined length is not a multiple of four, the result can be fractional.
- Negative or non-numeric inputs pass straight through the arithmetic and give a meaningless or not-a-number result.
- It never throws.

queries.need: Decode a string in bcrypt's base64 alphabet (./A-Za-z0-9) into an array of byte values, stopping after a requested number of bytes or at truncated or invalid input. A non-positive count throws an error.
queries.description:
This decodes a string written in a base64-style encoding back into raw byte values. It stops once it has produced a requested number of bytes.

**Inputs and output**
- It takes the encoded text and a positive count of how many bytes are wanted.
- It returns an array of numbers, one per decoded byte. The array may be shorter than requested.
- If the count is zero or negative, it throws an error whose message includes the offending value.

**How it decodes**
- It reads the text in groups of up to four characters.
- Each character is mapped to a 6-bit value through an external lookup table. The table may use a non-standard alphabet, such as the one bcrypt uses.
- Characters whose code falls outside the table are treated as invalid.
- Each group of four 6-bit values yields up to three 8-bit bytes:
  - First byte: all six bits of the first character plus the top two bits of the second.
  - Second byte: the low four bits of the second character plus the middle four bits of the third.
  - Third byte: the low two bits of the third character plus all six bits of the fourth.
- Each byte is briefly held as a one-character string and then converted back to its numeric code.

**When it stops early**
- Fewer than two characters remain at the start of a group.
- Either of the first two characters in a group is invalid.
- The third character is invalid.
- The requested byte count has been reached.
- The input runs out partway through a group.

In every case, the bytes produced so far are kept, so truncated or malformed input gives a shorter result rather than an error. Characters after an invalid one are ignored.

**Quirk: the fourth character is not validated**
- If the fourth character of a group is invalid, its "invalid" marker is negative one, which is combined directly into the third byte.
- That produces an out-of-range value (likely 65535) instead of stopping. This byte still counts toward the requested length.

queries.need: Convert a camelCase or PascalCase string to snake_case by replacing each ASCII capital letter A-Z with an underscore followed by its lowercase form. No grouping of acronyms and no trimming of a leading underscore.
queries.description:
This function takes a single text value and returns a new string where every uppercase letter is replaced by an underscore followed by that letter in lowercase. In practice it converts camel-case or Pascal-case names into lowercase, underscore-separated ones. For example, a word like "backgroundColor" becomes "background_color". The original string is not modified.

**Edge cases:**

- **Empty or no capitals:** An empty string comes back empty. A string with no capital letters comes back unchanged.
- **Leading capital:** If the string starts with a capital letter, the result starts with an underscore. "UserName" becomes "_user_name".
- **Consecutive capitals:** These are not grouped as a word. Each one gets its own underscore, so an acronym like "HTTP" becomes "_h_t_t_p".
- **Only basic Latin capitals:** Only the letters A through Z are affected. Accented or other non-ASCII uppercase characters, digits, spaces, and punctuation pass through untouched.
- **Existing underscores:** These are not merged or cleaned up. A capital right after an underscore produces a double underscore.

**Errors:** The input is not validated. A string works as expected. A value without the built-in text-substitution method, such as `null`, `undefined`, a number, or a plain object, makes the function throw a TypeError.

queries.need: Build a new date from a value (timestamp, string, or date) so that it matches the kind of a reference date. A function reference acts as a factory, an object with a construction-symbol hook uses that hook, and a Date or Date subclass reference uses its own constructor. Any other reference falls back to a plain Date.

inputs.name: reference
inputs.type: Date | function | object | null | undefined | number | string

queries.description:
This function creates a new date that matches the "kind" of a reference date. It takes two inputs: a reference (a date-like thing, or something that describes how to build one) and a value to turn into a date, such as a timestamp, a string, or another date. It returns the newly built date.

It decides how to build the result by checking the reference in this order:

1. **A function.** The reference is treated as a factory. It is called with the value, and whatever it returns is the result.
2. **An object with a special construction hook.** If the reference is a non-null object that carries a particular well-known symbol-keyed method, that method is called with the value. This lets custom date types, such as time-zone-aware dates, control how new instances are made.
3. **A real date instance.** If the reference is a built-in date or a subclass of one, it creates a new instance of the reference's own class from the value. A subclass therefore produces another instance of that subclass, not a plain date.
4. **Anything else.** This includes null, undefined, numbers and strings. It falls back to building an ordinary built-in date from the value.

**Edge cases and errors:**

- In the fallback case the reference only signals that a plain date is wanted. Its own contents are not used.
- The function does no validation. If the value can't be parsed, the result is whatever the chosen constructor or factory produces, which for a built-in date is an "invalid date" rather than a thrown error.
- Any exception thrown by a supplied factory, hook or subclass constructor passes straight through to the caller uncaught.

queries.need: Compute the Levenshtein edit distance between two strings: the minimum number of single-character insertions, deletions, and substitutions needed to turn one into the other. Characters are compared as UTF-16 code units.
queries.description:
This function computes the edit distance (Levenshtein distance) between two strings. That is the minimum number of single-character insertions, deletions, and substitutions needed to turn one string into the other. It returns a non-negative integer.

**Order of arguments.** It first swaps the inputs if needed so the longer string is treated as the primary one. Edit distance is symmetric, so the order you pass the strings in does not affect the result.

**Empty input.** If the shorter string is empty, it returns the length of the longer string, since that many insertions or deletions are required. If both strings are empty, the result is zero.

**Main computation.** For non-empty inputs, it hands off to one of two helpers. Judging by their names, both implement Myers' bit-parallel algorithm, which tracks the dynamic-programming state in the bits of machine integers:
- If the longer string is at most 32 characters, it uses a helper specialized for strings that fit in one 32-bit word.
- If the longer string is over 32 characters, it uses a general helper that presumably spans several words.

The choice between them is purely about performance; both should give the same answer.

**Errors and limitations.**
- There is no validation. If either argument lacks a length property, for example null or undefined, accessing it throws a runtime error.
- Other non-string values that do have a length would pass the checks, and how they behave depends on the helpers.
- The helpers almost certainly compare UTF-16 code units, not user-perceived characters. Emoji or other characters outside the Basic Multilingual Plane may therefore count as two units each, which can inflate the distance.

queries.need: Resolve an RFC 6901 JSON Pointer (e.g. "/users/0/name") against a nested object or array and return the value found there. Return undefined if an intermediate step is missing or not an object, and throw if the container is not an object.
queries.description:
This function looks up a value inside a nested data structure using a JSON Pointer path, in the style of RFC 6901, such as a slash-separated path like "/users/0/name".

**Inputs:** It takes two things:
- a container to search, which should be an object or an array
- a path, which goes through a helper that turns it into a list of segments. The helper likely accepts a slash-delimited string or an already-split list, and probably checks that the path is valid.

**Validation:** If the first argument is not of object type, it throws an error saying the input object is invalid. This check uses the language's type test, which reports null as an object. So null gets through. If the path then has any segments, reading a property of null fails with a native type error.

**Empty path:** The parsed path always starts with an empty placeholder segment, which is skipped. If that placeholder is the only segment (an empty path), the function returns the original container unchanged.

**Walking the path:** Otherwise it goes through the remaining segments in order. For each one:
- It first unescapes the segment. Standard pointer escaping means "~1" becomes a slash and "~0" becomes a tilde.
- It then uses the segment as a property name or array index to step one level deeper.

**Return value:**
- After the final segment, it returns whatever value it found there. This can be any type, including a primitive, null, or undefined if the key doesn't exist.
- If an intermediate step reaches something that is not a non-null object, it stops early and returns undefined instead of throwing. This covers a missing key, a number, a string, or null partway along the path.

queries.need: Return a new array of the enumerable property names of a value as strings. For arrays, arguments objects, buffers and typed arrays, list every index from 0 to length-1 first (sparse holes included), then any other own keys, optionally including inherited enumerable keys.
queries.description:
This function builds a list of the enumerable property names of an array-like value. It takes two inputs: the value to inspect, and a flag that controls whether properties inherited through the prototype chain are included.

**What it returns:** a new array of property names, all as strings.

**How it works:**

1. It classifies the value as one of: a true array, an arguments object, a binary buffer, or a typed array. These checks run in order, and each one runs only if the earlier ones failed.

2. If the value is any of those four kinds, the result starts with every numeric position from zero up to one less than the value's length, each converted to a string. This means the indexes are always present and in order, even for sparse positions that a normal key enumeration would skip. If the value is none of those kinds, the result starts empty.

3. It then walks every enumerable key the value exposes, including inherited ones. A key is added only if it passes two tests:
   - **Ownership:** it must belong directly to the object, unless the caller asked for inherited properties too.
   - **Not redundant or noisy (indexed values only):**
     - Keys that look like valid indexes within the length are skipped, since they were already added up front.
     - The length key is skipped, because some older Safari versions wrongly make it enumerable on argument objects.
     - For buffers, keys naming the offset and parent are skipped, because older Node.js exposes them as enumerable.
     - For typed arrays, keys naming the underlying storage, its byte length, and its byte offset are skipped, because older PhantomJS exposes them as enumerable.

**Edge cases:**

- For ordinary objects, the function simply collects own (or all, if requested) enumerable keys in enumeration order, with no index handling.
- For array-like values, any extra non-index properties attached by the user (for example, a custom named property on an array) appear after all the index keys.
- No errors are thrown deliberately. Passing null or undefined produces an empty list, since enumerating such a value yields nothing and none of the type checks match.

queries.need: Check whether a value is a primitive number that is a positive, finite whole number. Return strictly true or false; non-numbers such as numeric strings, booleans and boxed numbers give false.
queries.description:
This function checks whether a value is a positive whole number. It takes a single value of any type and returns a strict true or false. It returns true only when the value is a primitive number that is a whole number, greater than zero, and finite.

**Inputs that return true**
- Ordinary positive integers such as one, seven or a million.
- Very large values like 1e300. At that size every representable number is technically whole, so the check passes even though such numbers are far beyond the range where integers are exactly representable.

**Inputs that return false**
- **Zero, negative zero, and NaN.** These fail the opening truthiness test.
- **Other empty or falsy values:** an empty string, null, undefined, and the boolean false. These also fail the truthiness test.
- **Negative integers and fractional numbers**, such as 2.5.
- **Positive infinity.** It counts as whole when rounded down and is greater than zero, but it fails the final finiteness test. That is the only input that reaches the last test and fails there.
- **Negative infinity.** It fails the greater-than-zero test.
- **Numeric strings like "5".** Rounding converts the string to a number, but the comparison uses strict equality, so a string never equals a number.
- **The boolean true.** It rounds to one but is not strictly equal to one.
- **Boxed number objects and other objects.** An object is never strictly equal to a primitive number.

**Side effects and errors**
- For objects, rounding still converts the object to a number first. Any custom conversion method the object defines will run, even though the result is always false.
- A nonzero big-integer value throws a type error instead of returning false. Big integers cannot be converted to ordinary numbers by the rounding step. A big-integer zero is falsy, so it returns false without reaching that step.
- A symbol also throws a type error at the rounding step.

queries.need: Convert a millisecond duration into a long-form human-readable string using the largest fitting unit (days, hours, minutes, seconds), rounded and pluralized, keeping the sign. Values under one second come back as the raw number followed by " ms".
queries.description:
This function takes a duration in milliseconds and returns a human-readable string in long form, using the largest unit that fits.

**How it picks the unit**

It looks at the magnitude of the input, ignoring sign, and checks units from largest to smallest:

1. Days, if the duration is at least one day.
2. Hours, if it is at least one hour.
3. Minutes, if it is at least one minute.
4. Seconds, if it is at least one second.

The unit lengths are constants defined outside the function, presumably the number of milliseconds in each unit.

**How a matching unit is formatted**

The work is handed to a helper defined elsewhere. That helper typically:
- divides the value by the unit and rounds it to a whole number,
- attaches the full English unit name,
- makes the name plural when the magnitude is large enough. In the well-known library this pattern comes from, the cutoff is about one and a half units or more.

Example results would be "3 days", "1 hour" or "-2 minutes".

**Under one second**

If the magnitude is below one second, the function returns the raw input followed by a space and "ms", for example "250 ms". This value is not rounded, so fractions appear exactly as given.

**Edge cases**

- **Negative durations:** The unit is chosen by absolute value, but the original signed value is what gets formatted, so the sign is kept.
- **Bad input:** The function has no error handling. Non-numeric or missing input is not rejected.
  - Something that converts to a number may fall through to a unit branch.
  - Anything that compares as not-a-number falls straight to the last branch, giving results like "NaN ms" or "undefined ms".
- **Infinite values:** These land in the day branch, and the result depends on how the helper handles them.

queries.need: Given an array of version-constraint objects (each having an intersects(other, options) method) and an options value, return true if every distinct pair of constraints overlaps, false as soon as any pair does not. The input array must not be modified.
queries.description:
This function checks whether every pair in a collection of version constraints is mutually compatible. It is the kind of helper a semantic-versioning library uses to decide whether a set of constraints could all be satisfied at once.

**Inputs**
- An array of constraint objects. Each one must be able to report whether it overlaps with another constraint.
- An options value, passed unchanged to every overlap check. It typically carries flags such as loose parsing or prerelease handling.

**Output**
A boolean:
- **True** if every distinct pair of constraints overlaps.
- **False** as soon as any pair is found that does not overlap.

**How it works**
1. It makes a shallow copy of the array, so the caller's array is never modified.
2. It removes the last constraint from the copy and checks it against every constraint still left.
3. If all those checks pass, it removes the next constraint from the end and repeats against the shrinking remainder.
4. This continues until the copy is exhausted or a check fails. Each unordered pair is tested exactly once.

**Edge cases and errors**
- An empty array, or an array with one element, yields true, because there are no pairs to compare.
- Evaluation short-circuits. Once a non-overlapping pair is found, no further comparisons are made, both within the current round and across later rounds.
- The function does no validation or error handling of its own. If an element is missing the overlap-checking capability, or is null or undefined, the call will throw a runtime error. Any exception raised during an overlap check propagates to the caller.

queries.need: Build an adjacency map from a list of directed edge pairs [from, to]: every node seen as a source or a destination becomes a key, and its value is the set of nodes it points to directly. Sinks get empty sets, and duplicate edges collapse.
queries.description:
This function turns a list of directed connections into an adjacency lookup.

**Input:** an array of pairs. Each pair is read as a directed link from its first element to its second.

**Output:** a new Map. Every value that appears anywhere in the input, as a source or a destination, becomes a key. Each key's value is a Set of the nodes it points directly to.

**How it builds the result:**
- It walks the pairs in order. For each pair, it first makes sure both endpoints have an entry, creating an empty Set for any endpoint not yet seen.
- It then adds the destination to the source's Set.
- A node that only ever appears as a destination ends up with an empty Set, so sinks are still represented.

**Edge cases:**
- **Empty input:** returns an empty Map.
- **Duplicate pairs:** collapse into one entry, because Sets ignore repeated members.
- **Self-loops:** a pair whose two elements are the same produces a node that lists itself.
- **Key matching:** nodes are compared by identity (SameValueZero). Primitives with equal values count as the same node. Distinct objects count as different nodes even if they look alike.
- **Extra elements:** anything beyond the first two positions of a pair is ignored.

**Errors:**
- There is no validation.
- A missing or non-array input, or any entry that is null or undefined, throws a TypeError when the code tries to read from it.
- A pair with fewer than two elements does not throw. The missing position is read as undefined, and undefined is silently used as a node.

queries.need: Convert a 16-byte version 1 (time-based) UUID into the version 6 layout. The timestamp is reordered most-significant first and the version nibble is set to 6, so the result sorts chronologically. The input is not validated, and missing bytes are treated as zero.
queries.description:
This function converts a 16-byte time-based UUID in the version 1 layout into the version 6 layout. It returns a new 16-byte unsigned byte array.

**Input.** It takes an indexable sequence of 16 bytes, typically a byte array. It assumes the standard version 1 layout:
- the low 32 bits of the 60-bit timestamp come first,
- then the middle 16 bits,
- then the high 12 bits, which share their 16-bit field with a version nibble.

**Conversion.** Version 6 stores the same timestamp in the opposite order, most significant part first, so the identifiers sort chronologically.
- **Output bytes 0–6:** The function takes the high 12 timestamp bits, ignoring the old version nibble. It follows them with the middle 16 bits and then the low 32 bits. It packs this 60-bit sequence across the first six bytes and half of the seventh, shifting by one nibble at each step.
- **Version nibble:** It places the value 6 in the upper half of the seventh byte. The lower half holds the low four bits of the input's third byte.
- **Eighth byte:** This is a direct copy of the input's fourth byte, which supplies the last eight bits of the timestamp.
- **Final eight bytes:** These are copied unchanged. They hold the variant bits, clock sequence and node identifier.

**Edge cases and errors.** The function does no validation and never throws.
- It does not check that the input is version 1, and the original version nibble is simply discarded.
- It does not check the input's length. If the input is shorter than 16 bytes, missing positions read as undefined. In the shifting and masking steps these behave as zero, and directly copied positions become zero in the typed array.
- Extra bytes beyond 16 are ignored.
- If the input is a plain array with out-of-range numbers, the masking limits most derived values. Directly copied values are reduced modulo 256 when stored.

queries.need: Normalize a value returned by a CommonJS require for ES-module-style default import. Return it unchanged if it is truthy and has a truthy __esModule flag; otherwise wrap it as {default: value}.
queries.description:
This is the small helper that compilers like Babel or TypeScript insert so that code written with ES module import syntax can consume CommonJS modules.

**Input:** one value, typically whatever a CommonJS-style require call returned.

**Output:**
- If the value is truthy and carries the marker flag that transpilers set on compiled ES modules, it is returned unchanged. It already has the expected shape, with its primary export on the standard property.
- Otherwise, a new plain object is returned. That object has one property, the one ES module syntax uses for a module's primary export, and its value is the original input. Later code can then read the primary export the same way for both kinds of module.

**Edge cases:**
- Falsy inputs (null, undefined, zero, an empty string, false) skip the flag check, so reading the flag on null or undefined never throws. They are simply wrapped.
- The flag only needs to be truthy, not strictly true.
- A non-object truthy value, such as a number or a string, is checked for the flag and then wrapped.

The function never throws and has no side effects. Apart from the pass-through case, the original value is never modified or copied, only referenced inside the new wrapper.

queries.need: Wrap any value in a new result object marked as 'dirty', meaning a usable value was produced but problems were recorded. The value is stored unchanged by reference, and the function never throws.
queries.description:
This is a small generic factory that wraps a value in a result object. It takes a single argument of any type and returns a new object with two properties:

- **A status marker** set to the word meaning "tainted" or "not clean."
- **The original argument**, passed through unchanged.

The return type is generic over the input, so the wrapper keeps the exact type of whatever value was supplied.

This pattern is common in validation and parsing libraries. A result marked this way usually means processing produced a usable value, but problems were recorded along the way. That sits between a clean success and an outright failure, so later steps can keep working with the value while knowing it is not fully trustworthy.

On edge cases and errors:
